PCI.BIO:
R. Soto, (IEEE Life Senior Member '22) received the Ph.D. degree in electrical engineering from the University of Texas, Arlington, in 1990. He is currently a visiting professor of the ECE Department at UTRGV Brownsville. He was an undergraduate director for research, a professor with the National School of Engineering and Sciences, and deputy director of the national Robotics Laboratory with Tecnológico de Monterrey, Monterrey, Mexico. His research interests are in the areas of robotics, nonlinear and neuro-fuzzy control for Biomechatronics. He has published in journals and conferences cited in Institute for Scientific Information Web and Scopus in the area of control systems and robotics. Dr. Soto has been a member of the National System of Researchers (SNI) in Mexico since 1993.

DSL.TITLE: Towards Trustworthy Federated Learning
DSL.COMMENT:
Federated learning is a collaborative training model in which multiple clients optimize a
global model by transmitting updates to a coordinating server while keeping raw data on-device, thereby reducing direct data exposure and enabling iterative global improvement.

To enhance trustworthiness within this setting, we employ two-sided norm-based screening(TNBS) that removes both abnormally large and abnormally small updates, pair it with a q-fair objective to emphasize high-loss (disadvantaged) clients, and enforce client-level differential privacy with (ε,δ) guarantees. Analytically and empirically, this combination improves robustness and fairness while clarifying the privacy–utility trade-off.

For hierarchical deployments, TS-FedNBS introduces a two-stage defense for FedEdge:
Norm-based screening at edge nodes and robust median aggregation at the server. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate resilience against Gaussian, inner-product, and omniscient attacks, approaching no-attack accuracy and highlighting the necessity of server-side robustness in hierarchical systems.

Finally, Fed-ETF advances Byzantine resilience via cosine-based trust scoring relative to a server reference, selective participation with trust-weighted aggregation, and EMA-based adaptation of client learning rates. Various experiments are conducted on non-IID data with adversarial contamination to demonstrate the method's performance.

DSL.TITLE: Robust and Uncertainty-Aware Image Classification Using Bayesian Vision Transformer Model
DSL.COMMENT: Transformer Neural Networks have emerged as the predominant architecture for addressing a wide range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks such as machine translation, speech recognition, sentiment analysis, text anomaly detection etc. This noteworthy achievement of Transformer Neural Networks in the NLP field has sparked growing interest in integrating and using Transformer models in computer vision tasks. The Vision Transformer (ViT) model efficiently captures long-range dependencies by employing a self-attention mechanism to transform different image data into meaningful, significant representations. Recently, the Vision Transformer (ViT) has exhibited incredible performance in solving image classification problems through the utilization of ViT models, thereby surpassing the capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). Deterministic Vision Transformer (ViT) models are prone to noise and adversarial attacks, thereby lacking the ability to provide reliable confidence or uncertainty estimates for their output predictions. However, the development of a robust Vision Transformer (ViT) model, which can quantify the confidence (or uncertainty) level in the output predictions for vision applications with high-risk implications, such as autonomous vehicles, medical imaging etc., has significant importance. To ensure the reliability of Vision Transformer (ViT) in crucial applications, Bayesian inference facilitates the generation of probabilistic predictions. In this work, we develop a robust image classification framework using the Bayesian Vision Transformer (Bayes-ViT), which provides output predictions and quantifies their associated uncertainty. The proposed Bayes-ViT model employs a variational inference framework and optimizes the variational posterior distribution over the model parameters using the evidence lower bound (ELBO) loss. The propagation of variational moments in Bayes-ViT’s sequential, non-linear layers is achieved by utilizing the first-order Taylor series approximation. The output of Bayes-ViT is a predictive distribution, with the mean representing the prediction and the covariance matrix providing information about the uncertainty. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate (1) the superior robustness of proposed models under noise and adversarial attacks in comparison to the deterministic ViT models and (2) the ability for self-evaluation by utilizing the discernible increase in prediction uncertainty when the developed model encountered high levels of random noise and adversarial attacks, which acts as a warning sign for crucial image classification tasks.

CONGRANT.TITLE: REU Site: Hands-On Undergraduate Research to Advancing Agricultural Robotics in the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.CONTENT_GOAL: GOAL 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The overarching goal of this REU-site is to recruit and train talented undergraduates by immersing them in meaningful, hands-on research experiences that build technical expertise, enhance problem-solving skills, and prepare them for graduate studies and STEM careers. Central to this goal is engaging students in core robotics research areas—motion planning, sensor integration, control, localization, and human-robot interaction—while grounding these efforts in the specific needs and operational constraints of the RGV region. The program prioritizes the development of transferable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, and communication, recognizing that these outcomes are the most enduring benefits of research participation. While groundbreaking discoveries are welcomed, the program's true mission is to equip students with the knowledge, mindset, and abilities needed for advanced study and impactful STEM careers.

The proposed REU-site seeks support for three annual summer cohorts of undergraduate students. Each year, ten students will join UTRGV for a ten-week immersive, research-focused experience in which the design and mock field-testing of robotic systems naturally immerse students in core robotics research topics while supporting broader exploration beyond the prototypes themselves. REU participants will work collaboratively in interdisciplinary teams and alongside UTRGV's graduate student population.

Through this structure, the program aims to achieve the following objectives:

Intellectual Focus: To conduct research in robotics aimed at advancing motion planning, sensor integration, control, and human-robot collaboration for systems intended to operate under the environmental conditions and operational constraints commonly found in rural and agricultural regions of the RGV.

Educational Objective: To provide research opportunities for undergraduates—particularly those from the RGV, enabling them to contribute to solving regionally relevant engineering challenges while deepening their engagement through hands-on projects that connect directly to local agricultural and rural needs.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaboration of Multi-robot for Autonomous Tasks
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A multi-robot collaboration is proposed using computer vision and automatic control to perform autonomous tasks with logistics and delivery applications. A cooperative behavior between ground and aerial robots will be implemented as a testbed, leveraging the strengths of each robot. Experimental results show the proposed collaborative system's proof of concept and effectiveness. Future research will focus on testing new control and communications algorithms using the experimental testbed and writing proposals for the NSF HSI programs for enriching learning and students' experiences.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: An Active Learning Didactic Proposal with Human-Computer Interaction in Engineering Education: A Direct Current Motor Case Study
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Engineering education requires learning strategies to engage students and improve the development of disciplinary and transversal competencies.

Additionally, as economic resources are generally limited, it is sought to avoid investing large sums of money in software and hardware, as well as in fitting out laboratories.

This work presents a didactic proposal within the framework of active and collaborative learning that includes the flipped classroom technique to be applied in the curriculum of undergraduate engineering programs and inside a massive flexible digital master class.

The activity is the mathematical modeling, simulation, and control system of a direct current motor where simulation work is carried out in open license computational packages. Students understand the physical phenomena involved in the motor’s modeling and the input–output variables’ relations.

Moreover, an analogy between an electromechanical and a pure electrical model is carried out, where the relevant variables respond in an agile and reliable manner. To validate the modeling, the differential equations are solved by applying numerical methods and tested for control purposes.

The activity has been validated with a rule-based system applied to a Likert scale survey data. This type of human–computer interaction, in the context of active learning, could engage students and motivate them to develop competencies that are highly appreciated by industry practitioners.

SERVICE_COLLEGE.DESC: The self-study is a comprehensive report that examines the status of the academic unit and its programs based on their activities and achievements since the previous review. The self-study must contain enough information for a preliminary evaluation of the academic unit’s quality. It also serves as a starting point for the external reviewers’ in-depth review of the academic unit and its program. This document should identify strengths and weaknesses in curriculum and instruction, student quality, educational outcomes, research activities and funding levels, resource availability and needs, and special features or services provided by the program. The self-study should also serve as a vehicle for the academic unit to plan and align with the University’s strategic plan. It should include mechanisms to address current and future challenges, build on current strengths, and maximize opportunities likely to develop within the academic unit and its program disciplines.
SERVICE_COLLEGE.ACCOMPLISH:
The self-study report and response after the visit of the external reviewers

I. The Academic Unit (ECE Department) to be completed by the academic unit as a whole. ​

II. The Academic Program (MSE in EE) with the Annual Program Review guidelines.

III. Unit Response report for the unit based on the reviewers' feedback, and develop action plans to address some of the recommendations.
